verdicts.strongest_argument: The facts are correct and I verified them independently (July 2026 adjusted NICS 1,061,883, +8.5% vs 978,731; Q1 FY2026 comps +2.1% with Hunting & Shooting +6.3%). But NSSF-adjusted NICS is the single most-published public datapoint in this sector: the July release was carried on 5 August by Outdoor Wire, Tactical Wire, Ammoland, GunsAmerica, OutdoorHub, NRA Women and TheFirearmBlog, several with explicit 'gun sales stay hot' framing. Anyone who owns a firearms retailer sees it monthly, and the June release on 6 July was covered the same way. What is genuinely NOT drawn out is the link to SPWH's own Q2 estimate line, and I concede that: the 2026-08-30 StockStory/Yahoo preview has consensus revenue flat YoY (about $296.7m against $293.9m) and states analysts 'generally reconfirmed their estimates over the last 30 days', with no mention of NICS or firearms demand anywhere in it. So the data is loudly published and the SPWH implication is not. That is the 45-65 band, and I put it in the upper half of it because the publication is headline trade press rather than obscure, and because the magnitude is directly contested by the mix/margin findings below - the same accelerating demand is SPWH's lowest-margin demand lapping a 32.0% gross margin, so the EBITDA translation of a revenue beat is much smaller than the revenue translation. Separately, the NICS-to-SPWH mapping is looser than the finding implies in both directions: in Q2 FY2025 NICS was falling YoY while SPWH still printed +2.1% comps and H&S +4%, and in Q1 FY2026 H&S ran ~4 points above NICS. The series sets a direction, not a coefficient.

verdicts.baseline_evidence: This is where I have to be plain: with 23 contracts of total open interest and no two-sided ATM, the baseline contains no measured statement of what is priced. The only tape evidence is a +3.04% 20-day run-up against 28.3% annualised realised vol - a 20-day sigma of about 8.0%, so +3.04% is roughly 0.4 sigma and statistically indistinguishable from no move at all. I cannot treat that as a lean and I am not going to. It weakly supports the hunter, not me. My 58 rests on publication of the data plus contest over its magnitude, not on the price having moved.
verdicts.what_would_change_it: A sell-side note or financial-press article between 6 July and today that explicitly raised SPWH Q2 numbers on the June/July NICS prints would push this to 80; evidence that SPWH's July comps decoupled from NICS would move it the other way.

verdicts.strongest_argument: I checked the year on the source as instructed: the URL path is /2025/03/12/ and the Silencer Central drop-ship release is genuinely a 2025 document that predates the tax change - the hunter's date discipline is sound. But every macro leg of this is in the wire copy. The $0 NFA transfer tax effective 1 January 2026 is documented by SilencerCo, CMMG, Silencer Shop's dedicated '$0 NFA Tax Stamp Hub' and multiple trade explainers, and the NFA check surge was literally the headline on Ammoland's July write-up: 'July Gun Sales Rise 8.5% as NFA Checks More Than Double'. The suppressor boom as an investable theme has been written up against Ruger by name. What is unpublished is only the SPWH-specific arithmetic - and my primary objection is not that it is priced, it is that it is too small to matter. NFA checks are not suppressor units (they include SBRs, AOWs and other transfers), the SPWH channel is a third-party drop-ship where Silencer Central performs the transfer and ships, so the economics are a split or a referral rather than a full-margin retail sale, and SPWH has never quantified it in a release, a 10-Q or on a call. The hunter reads management's total silence on the Q1 call as concealed upside; the simpler reading, for a company that badly needs a good story and instead named hunting/shooting, fishing and personal protection as its pillars, is that it is not material. Even a generous share of a roughly $250-300m/quarter national suppressor retail pool is low-single-digit millions of revenue on a ~$300m quarter.

verdicts.baseline_evidence: None usable. No chain, and a 0.4-sigma 20-day run-up says nothing either way. The absence of a run-up does not rescue the finding because my objection is size, not novelty.
verdicts.what_would_change_it: Any SPWH disclosure sizing suppressor or NFA-adjacent revenue at more than about 2% of quarterly sales, or management flagging it as a growth driver tonight, and this becomes a real finding rather than a small one.

verdicts.strongest_argument: Two separate failures, and I want to keep them apart. First, on pricing: this was not a quiet 8-K. SPWH issued a press release, 'Sportsman's Warehouse Extends and Restructures Key Credit Facilities', and it was carried on 24 June 2026 by TipRanks, The Globe and Mail, TradingView ('Sportsman's Warehouse Refinances ABL Term Loan to 2031, Amends Revolver With Wells Fargo') and StockTitan, and posted on the company's own IR newsroom. That is wire copy, ten weeks before this print and well outside the 20-day window, so whatever repricing it deserved is in the base. Second, and more seriously, the causal premise is factually wrong. I checked what actually drove the two extreme prints. The -29.8% on 4 December 2025 was a full-year adjusted EBITDA guidance cut to $22-26m against roughly $34.6m consensus on a warning that consumer spending softened from mid-October, with Q3 revenue and EPS in line. The +97.9% on 1 April 2025 was a Q4 adjusted EBITDA beat ($14.6m vs $5.3m), a $27.3m net-debt reduction and a positive comp outlook. Both were guidance and EBITDA events, not maturity events. Extending a revolver to 2031 removes a date; it does not remove the mechanism that produced either move, and that mechanism is fully live tonight - SPWH is carrying a reaffirmed $30-36m FY EBITDA guide against -$8.1m in Q1, which is exactly the setup that produced December. So the finding, if believed, would cause a reader to narrow the tail at precisely the print where the tail should not be narrowed. I accept the fact and reject the inference.

verdicts.baseline_evidence: The stock sits at $1.185, 5.8% above its 52-week low and 64.9% below its 52-week high, ten weeks after the refinancing was press-released. Either the market absorbed it or it decided the maturity date was never the binding constraint on this equity - both readings kill the claim that the price still 'embeds' the wall. There is no chain to check, so I am relying on publication plus the level, not on a dated move I can point to.
verdicts.what_would_change_it: Evidence that the December 2025 or April 2025 reactions were actually driven by covenant or availability disclosures rather than by the EBITDA guide would restore the premise; I found the opposite in both cases.

verdicts.strongest_argument: I accept every fact here - I verified the 29.6% vs 30.4% gross margin, the -$8.1m Q1 adjusted EBITDA, and the $30-36m FY guide directly off the 2 June press release, and the back-half loading is arithmetic on that guide. That is the problem. All three legs are restatements of documents that were published and widely covered, and the guidance leg specifically 'restates published guidance', which my scale puts at 90-100. The Academy leg is also public: on the 9 June 2026 call (the finding says 10 June) management said sales through Memorial Day were up low single digits with comparable sales roughly flat and a 'little bit of a slowdown', and that gas prices are a headwind pulling roughly $17.5bn/month out of discretionary spend - written up by SGB Media as 'Academy Returns to Positive Comps, Sees Gas Prices Restraining FY Spend' and by MarketBeat/Yahoo in their Q1 call highlights. ASO is a multi-billion-dollar covered name, not an obscure source. The specific phrase '$4+ gas prices' I could not verify and it looks like an embellishment; what is verifiable is 'gas prices definitely are a headwind'. Note also that Academy's overall print was strong - comps +2.9%, sales +6.7%, raised the low end of guidance, stock up - so quoting only the QTD softness selects one side of a two-sided read-across. Decisively, the soft-consumer view is already in the numbers the market is trading against: consensus has SPWH Q2 revenue roughly flat YoY versus the +2.8% it just delivered, which is analysts embedding exactly this deceleration. The 15 points I withhold are for the framing that the FY EBITDA guide is now arithmetically dependent on a very large back half, which is true and is the live risk tonight even if every input is public.

Academy management on the Q1 FY2026 call: comps roughly flat quarter-to-date through Memorial Day, gas prices a headwind restraining full-year spend.

verdicts.baseline_evidence: Consensus revenue of roughly $296.7m, flat YoY against a quarter that just grew 2.8%, is the clearest available evidence that the soft-consumer case is in the numbers. I cannot corroborate with a put skew because there is no chain, and the +3.95% 5-day / +3.04% 20-day tape is 0.4 sigma - it neither confirms nor denies a bearish lean. My number here rests on publication and on consensus, and I say so.
verdicts.what_would_change_it: If the finding produced a quantified Q2 gross-margin estimate materially below anything published - rather than restating Q1's 80bp and the FY guide - the framing would earn a lower score.

verdicts.strongest_argument: This is the same claim as SPWH-a#0 read off the same monthly NSSF series, and it should not be scored as independent information - see interactions. It scores marginally higher than a#0 because it adds no mechanism, only the arithmetic on the same three published monthly releases, and because one of its company figures is wrong: it states SPWH printed '+7.4% hunting-and-shooting' in fiscal Q1, whereas the 2 June press release and 8-K state Hunting and Shooting Sports same-store sales increased 6.3%. That is a small error, it does not overturn the thesis, and a#0 has it right - but it means the two hunters are not independently corroborating each other on the company side. The substance I concede is the same substance I conceded on a#0: the +7.7% fiscal-Q2 NICS aggregate against roughly +2.3% in fiscal Q1 is real, it maps to a quarter that ended 1 August 2026 and therefore lands squarely inside tonight's print, and I found no publication connecting it to SPWH's Q2 estimates - the 30 August preview has consensus flat and no mention of firearms demand at all. What holds the number at 60 rather than lower is that the input data is headline trade press covered by at least six outlets on 5 August, and that the EBITDA translation is contested by the gross-margin lap in b#1, which is the same demand read on a different line.

verdicts.strongest_argument: The fact is right and I verified it independently, but not from the source given - the cited URL (accession 0000950170-25-080929) is the Q1 FY2025 press release for the thirteen weeks ended 3 May 2025, not the 4 September 2025 Q2 release, so the citation does not support the 32.0% figure even though the figure is correct. Q2 FY2025 was net sales $293.9m, comps +2.1%, gross margin 32.0% - up 80bp from 31.2% on healthier inventory and higher-margin fishing - and adjusted EBITDA $8.3m. Both halves of the comparison are therefore in company press releases that were reported at the time (the Q2 FY2025 release on 4 September 2025 across Globe and Mail, Yahoo, GuruFocus and SGB; the Q1 FY2026 release on 2 June 2026), and the claim is one subtraction away from them. That is 'published results restated'. I withhold 18 points because the specific framing - that this is the hardest gross-margin comp in the recent run and that the very mix now accelerating is what compressed margin last quarter - is a sharp observation I did not find written up anywhere ahead of this print, and it is the single best argument against the bull case in this brief. On size I am with the direction and slightly ahead of the implied magnitude: 32.0% was flattered by fishing mix and clean inventory, and a firearms/ammunition-heavy Q2 plausibly lands 100-150bp below it, which on roughly $300m of sales is $3-4.5m of gross profit - enough to neutralise most of the gross-profit benefit of the revenue beat that a#0 and b#0 are arguing for.

verdicts.baseline_evidence: Consensus at roughly flat revenue and EPS of about -$0.08 already assumes a weak quarter, which is partial evidence the margin risk is embedded. No chain means I cannot show puts bid, and I will not pretend the +3% run-up is a skew. My score here is publication-driven.
verdicts.what_would_change_it: Evidence that the fishing and clean-inventory tailwinds that drove the 32.0% are repeating this year would cut the size; a company comment that firearms mix is now margin-accretive would cut it further.

verdicts.strongest_argument: Same document, same event and substantially the same claim as SPWH-a#2 - it should not be counted twice. The refinancing was press-released by the company on 24 June 2026 and carried the same day by TipRanks, The Globe and Mail, TradingView and StockTitan; it is not a filing that only a diligent reader found. The added detail - Q1 liquidity of $116.7m against a minimum-availability covenant of the greater of $30m or 10% of the gross borrowing base - comes straight out of the 10-Q filed 2 June, also public. The load-bearing part of the claim is the assertion that 'the near-term maturity wall the price appears to embed is gone', and that assertion has no support I can find: with 23 contracts of total open interest there is no instrument in this name from which anyone can read what the price embeds, and the fact that the stock is 5.8% above its 52-week low ten weeks after the refinancing was announced argues the maturity date was never what the equity was discounting. What is discounting the equity is $22-26m of realised FY2025 EBITDA against a $30-36m FY2026 guide, -$8.1m in Q1, and a $1.18 share price - a leverage and earnings problem, not a calendar problem. Fact accepted, inference rejected.

verdicts.baseline_evidence: Spot $1.185, 5.8% off the 52-week low and 64.9% off the high, ten weeks after the announcement. No chain to read. The absence of any sustained re-rating after a press-released maturity extension is the strongest thing I have, and it cuts against the claim that the price still carries the wall.
verdicts.what_would_change_it: A dated intraday move on 24 June 2026 showing the market did not react at all, combined with a going-concern or covenant reference still live in the Q2 10-Q, would make me reconsider whether the refinancing is genuinely unabsorbed.

interactions: Three of the four claim-pairs here are duplicates, and one pair is a mirror. (1) SPWH-a#0 and SPWH-b#0 are one claim - the same NSSF-adjusted NICS monthly series aggregated over the same fiscal Q2 window, with identical May/June/July figures and identical arithmetic. They are cited to two different Outdoor Wire pages (the June release and the July release) but that is one data source, not two. Their size_check values are NOT additive; treat +11 as the total for the demand-acceleration claim, not +22. They also disagree on a verifiable company number: a#0 says Q1 Hunting and Shooting was +6.3% (correct per the 2 June release) and b#0 says +7.4% (wrong). Because they are the same claim, that is a defect in b#0, not corroboration. (2) SPWH-a#2 and SPWH-b#2 are one claim on one document - the 18 June 2026 amendments, filed 24 June. a#2 cites the StockTitan mirror and b#2 cites the EDGAR original; both were press-released by the company the same day. Do not count the refinancing twice, and note both share the same defect: the load-bearing inference (that the reaction distribution is now narrower, or that the price 'embeds' a maturity wall) is unsupported, and in a#2's case demonstrably wrong on causation, since the -29.8% and +97.9% prints were EBITDA-guidance events. (3) SPWH-a#3's first leg and SPWH-b#1 are the same gross-margin/mix claim, both resting on the 2 June 2026 Q1 press release, with b#1 adding the Q2 FY2025 32.0% lap. (4) The mirror, and the most important interaction in the brief: a#0/b#0 and a#3/b#1 are the SAME demand series read on two different P&L lines with opposite signs. The NICS acceleration drives firearms and ammunition, which the company itself named as the cause of the 80bp Q1 gross-margin contraction, into a quarter lapping the highest gross margin of the recent run. A revenue beat of 3-5% at 22-25% incremental margin generates roughly $3m of gross profit; a 100-150bp margin miss against 32.0% on ~$300m destroys $3-4.5m. The two largely cancel at the EBITDA line, which is what a $1.18 levered equity trades on. Any ranking that adds the bull findings and the bear findings as independent contributions will double-count one demand series and overstate the net edge in whichever direction it happens to weight more heavily. Finally, a general caveat that applies to all seven: with 23 contracts of total open interest there is no measured statement of what this name has priced. Every high score I have given rests on prior publication with a dated URL, and every low-to-mid score rests on my failure to find such publication - not on the +3.04% 20-day run-up, which at roughly 0.4 sigma against 28.3% realised vol is indistinguishable from no move and must not be read as a lean.
